hello.title: Hello, Erlang
hello.summary: Write your first Erlang program: a module with a main function that prints text with io:format.
hello.lesson.0: **Erlang** is a language for systems that must run for years without stopping, such as chat servers and phone networks. An Erlang program is made of **modules**, and every module contains **functions**.
hello.lesson.2: Save this program as `hello.erl` and run it in a terminal with `escript hello.erl`. The tool `escript` comes with Erlang. It reads the file and calls the function `main`. The first line `#!/usr/bin/env escript` marks the file as a script. Every complete program in this course is run this way.
hello.lesson.3: Lines that start with `-` are **attributes**. `-module(hello).` gives the module its name. `-export([main/1]).` makes the function `main` usable from outside the module. `main/1` means: the function `main` with **one** argument. This number is called the **arity**.
hello.lesson.4: `main(_) ->` starts the function. `escript` passes the command-line arguments as the one argument; the `_` means that you ignore it. After the arrow `->` comes the body. The period `.` ends the function, and every attribute ends with a period too.
hello.lesson.6: `io:format(...)` calls the function `format` from the module `io`. The colon `:` separates the module name from the function name. The text goes in double quotes. `~n` inside the text starts a new line.
hello.lesson.8: A body can have several **expressions**. A comma `,` separates them, and they run from top to bottom. Only the last one ends with the period.
hello.lesson.9: To print values, write `~p` in the text and give the values as a second argument: a **list** in square brackets `[...]`. Each `~p` is replaced by the next value from the list. Erlang calculates `2 + 3` before it prints.
hello.lesson.11: Without `~n` the next output continues on the same line. `io:format("a")` followed by `io:format("b~n")` prints `ab`.
hello.lesson.12: Watch the punctuation: a period in the middle of a body ends the function too early, and the next line is then an error. Between expressions you need a comma.
hello-1.options.1: It is version 1 of the function
hello-1.options.2: It is the first function in the module
hello-1.explain: The number after `/` is the arity: how many arguments the function takes.
hello-2.explain: Each `~p` prints the next value from the list. There is no space between them, so you see `42`.
hello-3.explain: Erlang calculates `10 + 5` first. `~p` is replaced by `15`.

hello-4.explain: The first call prints `a` without `~n`, so `b` follows on the same line.

hello-6.explain: An export names a function with its arity. `main(_)` has one argument, so it is `main/1`.

hello-7.explain: First the module and function, then the text with `~p~n`, then the list with the value.

hello-8.explain: The script line comes first, then `-module` and `-export`, then the function `main`.

values.title: Values and types
values.summary: Calculate with integers and floats, and get to know atoms, booleans, strings and binaries.
values.lesson.0: Erlang calculates with `+`, `-` and `*`. The operator `/` always gives a **float** (a decimal number), even when the result is whole. For whole numbers, `div` divides without the rest and `rem` gives the rest.
values.lesson.2: A float needs a digit on both sides of the point: write `0.5`, not `.5`. `round` rounds a float to the nearest integer, and `trunc` cuts off the decimals. Integers have no size limit, so you can calculate with very big numbers.
values.lesson.5: An **atom** is a constant whose value is its own name, such as `ok`, `error` or `red`. Atoms start with a lowercase letter. Words that start with an uppercase letter are variables; you meet them in the next unit.
values.lesson.7: The booleans are the atoms `true` and `false`. You compare with `==`, `/=` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `>=` and `=<` (careful: not `<=`). `==` treats `1` and `1.0` as equal; `=:=` also compares the type. `and`, `or` and `not` combine booleans.
values.lesson.10: A string in double quotes like `"Hello"` is a **list of character codes**. `~s` prints it as text. `++` joins two lists, and `length` counts the elements. Because `~p` shows a list of character codes as text, `[72, 105]` prints as `"Hi"`.
values.lesson.12: A **binary** like `<<"Erlang">>` stores text as compact bytes. Modern Erlang code uses binaries for text a lot. `~s` prints binaries as text too, and `byte_size` counts the bytes.
values.card.4: `"hi"` is a list, `<<"hi">>` is a binary
values-1.explain: `div` divides whole numbers and drops the rest: 17 = 3 * 5 + 2.
values-2.explain: `rem` gives the rest of the division: 17 = 3 * 5 + 2.
values-3.explain: `/` always gives a float, so `8 / 2` is `4.0`.
values-4.explain: `=:=` also compares the type. `1` is an integer and `1.0` is a float, so the result is `false`. `1 == 1.0` is `true`.
values-5.prompt: Which of these is an atom?
values-5.explain: Atoms start with a lowercase letter. `Ok` is a variable, `"ok"` is a string and `<<"ok">>` is a binary.

values-6.explain: `=<` means less than or equal, so `3 =< 3` is `true`. Erlang has no `<=` operator for numbers.
values-7.explain: `++` joins the lists to `"cats"`, which has 4 characters.

values-9.explain: `div` works only with integers, and `2.5` is a float. Use `10 / 2.5` instead.
values-10.prompt: Build the expression that gives the rest of 10 divided by 3.
values-10.explain: `rem` gives the rest of a whole-number division. `%` starts a comment in Erlang.
values-11.explain: A string is a list of character codes. `72` is `H` and `105` is `i`, so `~p` shows the list as `"Hi"`.
values-12.explain: Strings are lists, and `++` joins two lists. `+` works only with numbers.
matching.title: Variables and pattern matching
matching.summary: Bind values to variables once, and use pattern matching to take tuples and lists apart.
matching.lesson.0: A **variable** starts with an uppercase letter, for example `Name` or `Age`. The `=` gives it a value. We say the variable is **bound** to the value.
matching.lesson.2: A variable is bound only **once** and never changes. This is called **single assignment**. When you need a new value, you use a new name.
matching.lesson.4: `Count = Count + 1` does not add one. `Count` is already `5`, so Erlang checks `5 = 6`, which fails. The program stops with a `badmatch` error.
matching.lesson.5: This is because `=` is the **match operator**. The left side is a **pattern**. If it contains a variable without a value, the variable gets bound. If the variable already has a value, both sides must be equal. So `10 = X` works when `X` is `10`.
matching.lesson.7: A **tuple** groups a fixed number of values in curly braces, for example `{point, 3, 4}`. The first element is often an atom that says what the tuple is. `element(2, T)` returns the second element, and `tuple_size(T)` the number of elements.
matching.lesson.9: Pattern matching takes a tuple apart. The pattern `{point, X, Y}` matches any tuple with three elements whose first element is the atom `point`. `X` and `Y` get bound to the other two values.
matching.lesson.11: The underscore `_` matches any value and ignores it. Names that start with an underscore, such as `_Year`, also match anything; use them when you want to show what the value means. Lists in square brackets can be matched in the same way.
matching.lesson.13: Many Erlang functions return `{ok, Value}` when they succeed and `{error, Reason}` when they fail. With a pattern like `{ok, Value}` you take the result out and check for success in one step.
matching.card.2: `{point, X, Y} = P` takes a tuple apart

functions.title: Functions
functions.summary: Write your own functions with several clauses and guards, and store anonymous functions in variables.
functions.lesson.0: You write a function as `name(Arguments) -> Body.` and call it with `name(Values)`. A module can have many functions. `main` can call the other functions of the module directly; only functions called from outside need `-export`.
functions.lesson.2: Erlang has no `return` keyword. A function returns the value of its **last expression**. A function with two arguments has the arity 2, so the function below is `area/2`.
functions.lesson.5: A function can have several **clauses**. Each clause has its own pattern for the arguments, and a semicolon `;` separates the clauses. Erlang tries them from top to bottom and runs the first one that matches. The last clause ends with a period.
functions.lesson.7: Functions with the same name but a different arity are different functions. `greet/1` and `greet/2` can both exist in one module.
functions.lesson.9: A **guard** adds a condition to a clause. It starts with `when` after the arguments. The clause runs only when the pattern matches **and** the guard is `true`. Guards can use comparisons and tests like `is_integer(X)`.
functions.lesson.11: If no clause matches, the program stops with a `function_clause` error. Order the clauses from the most specific to the most general.
functions.lesson.12: An **anonymous function** has no name: `fun(X) -> X * 3 end`. You can store it in a variable and call it like a function. You can also pass it to another function as an argument.
functions.card.4: The last expression is the return value
functions-2.prompt: What is the arity of this function?
functions-2.explain: The function takes two arguments, `Width` and `Height`, so it is `area/2`.
functions-3.explain: `25` is not `0` and not less than `10`, so the last clause runs.
functions-4.explain: The arity is part of the function's identity. `f/1` and `f/2` are two different functions.

functions-6.explain: An anonymous function starts with `fun` and ends with `end`.

functions-10.explain: An anonymous function is `fun`, the arguments, `->`, the body and `end`.

lists.title: Lists
lists.summary: Take lists apart with [H | T], use lists:map, lists:filter and lists:sum, and write list comprehensions.
lists.lesson.0: A **list** holds any number of values: `[10, 20, 30]`. `length` counts the elements, `hd` returns the first element (the **head**), and `tl` returns the rest (the **tail**). `++` joins two lists.
lists.lesson.2: The pattern `[H | T]` splits a list into its head and its tail. The bar `|` separates the first element from the rest. You can also use `|` to build a list: `[0 | Nums]` puts `0` in front of `Nums`.
lists.lesson.4: The empty list `[]` has no head, so `[H | T] = []` fails. A list with one element has the empty list as its tail: `[x]` is the same as `[x | []]`.
lists.lesson.6: The module `lists` has many useful functions. `lists:sum` adds all numbers, `lists:max` finds the biggest, `lists:sort` sorts, `lists:reverse` reverses, and `lists:member` checks if a value is in the list.
lists.lesson.8: `lists:map(F, List)` calls the function `F` for every element and returns a list of the results. `lists:filter(F, List)` keeps only the elements for which `F` returns `true`. The function comes first, the list second.
lists.lesson.11: A **list comprehension** builds a new list in one line: `[X * X || X <- Nums]`. Read it as: the list of `X * X` for every `X` taken from `Nums`. The arrow `<-` takes the elements one by one. Conditions after a comma keep only some elements.
lists.card.4: `[X * 2 || X <- L, X > 0]` is a list comprehension

recursion.title: Recursion
recursion.summary: Repeat work with functions that call themselves, and use accumulators for tail recursion.
recursion.lesson.0: Erlang has no `for` or `while` loops. To repeat something, a function calls itself. This is called **recursion**.
recursion.lesson.2: Every recursive function needs a **base case**: a clause that stops. Here it is `countdown(0)`. The other clause makes the problem smaller (`N - 1`) and calls the function again.
recursion.lesson.3: Lists fit recursion well. The base case is the empty list `[]`. The other clause takes the list apart with `[H | T]` and calls itself with the tail.
recursion.lesson.5: Step by step: `sum([1, 2, 3])` is `1 + sum([2, 3])`, which is `1 + 2 + sum([3])`, which is `1 + 2 + 3 + sum([])`, and `sum([])` is `0`. Each call must wait for the next one, so a long list needs a lot of memory.
recursion.lesson.7: An **accumulator** is an extra argument that carries the result so far. `sum/1` starts the work by calling `sum/2` with `0`. Remember: `sum/1` and `sum/2` are different functions.
recursion.lesson.9: In `sum(T, Acc + H)` the recursive call is the **last** thing the function does. This is a **tail call**, and the function is **tail recursive**. Erlang does not need extra memory for tail calls. In `H + sum(T)` the addition comes after the call, so it is not a tail call.
recursion.lesson.11: When you build a list with an accumulator, each new element goes to the front with `[New | Acc]`. The result is then in reverse order, so the base case calls `lists:reverse`.
recursion.lesson.13: A recursion that never reaches its base case never stops. For example, `countdown(-1)` above never reaches `0`. A guard like `when N > 0` protects against this.
recursion.card.3: Accumulator: `sum([H | T], Acc) -> sum(T, Acc + H).`
recursion.card.4: Tail call: the recursive call is the last step

maps.title: Maps and tuples
maps.summary: Store key-value pairs in maps, read and update them, and use tagged tuples as small records.
maps.lesson.0: A **map** stores pairs of keys and values: `#{name => "Ada", age => 36}`. The arrow `=>` links a key to its value. Keys are often atoms. `maps:get(Key, Map)` returns the value, and `map_size` counts the pairs.
maps.lesson.2: If a key is missing, `maps:get(Key, Map)` stops the program with a `badkey` error. `maps:get(Key, Map, Default)` returns the default value instead. `maps:is_key` checks if a key exists.
maps.lesson.4: Maps never change, like variables. `maps:put(Key, Value, Map)` returns a **new** map with the pair added or replaced. The short form `Map#{Key => Value}` does the same. The old map stays as it was.
maps.lesson.6: You can take values out of a map with pattern matching. In a pattern you write `:=` instead of `=>`. The pattern matches when the map has these keys; other keys are ignored.
maps.lesson.8: `maps:to_list` returns all pairs as `{Key, Value}` tuples, and `maps:keys` returns the keys. The order is not fixed, so sort the result with `lists:sort` when the order matters.
maps.lesson.11: A tuple with an atom as its first element works like a small record: `{book, Title, Year}`. The atom is a **tag** that says what the data is. Functions can have one clause for each tag. Use a tuple for a few fixed fields and a map when you want named keys.
maps.card.2: `M#{b => 2}` or `maps:put(b, 2, M)` gives a new map
maps.card.3: `#{a := A} = M` takes a value out

processes.title: Processes
processes.summary: Start processes with spawn, send them messages with !, and wait for answers with receive.
processes.lesson.0: An Erlang program can run thousands of small **processes** at the same time. Each process has its own memory. Processes do not share variables; they work together by sending **messages**.
processes.lesson.1: `spawn(Fun)` starts a new process that runs the function `Fun`, and returns its **process identifier**, or **pid**. `self()` returns the pid of the process that is running the code. `is_pid` checks if a value is a pid.
processes.lesson.3: `Pid ! Message` sends a message to a process. A message can be any value. It goes into the **mailbox** of the receiving process. The sender does not wait.
processes.lesson.4: `receive` waits for a message and matches it against patterns, like the clauses of a function. The block ends with `end`. A process can also send a message to itself.
processes.lesson.6: To get an answer, send your own pid with the message, for example `{self(), 21}`. The other process uses this pid to reply. Here the new process doubles the number and sends back `{result, 42}`.
processes.lesson.8: A process that serves many messages runs a recursive **loop**. The argument of the loop is the state of the process. After each message, the loop calls itself with the new state. The atom `stop` ends the loop.
processes.lesson.10: Messages from one process to another arrive in the order they were sent. Messages from different processes can arrive in any order. That is why the examples wait for a reply before they print.
processes.lesson.11: `receive` can wait forever. With `after` you set a time limit in milliseconds. If no matching message arrives in time, the code after `after` runs.
processes.lesson.13: `receive` takes only messages that match one of its patterns. Other messages stay in the mailbox. If no message ever matches and there is no `after`, the process waits forever.
processes.card.2: `receive Pattern -> ... end` waits for a message
processes.card.3: `self()` is the pid of the current process
